Checklists by delivery format and meeting or event type

Start with the delivery format checklist, then use the checklist that matches your meeting or event type.

Use the checklist that matches your planning path. Each checklist summarizes the main actions to take before, during, and after the event.

If your meeting or event includes both in-person and remote participants, also review the hybrid meeting or event checklist.

Each checklist item includes practical guidance and a link to related guidance in the Best practices for accessible meetings and events guide (opens in a new tab) for topics that need more depth.

1.  Delivery format checklist

Start here to plan for how participants will attend: in person, virtually, or in a hybrid format.

1.1  In-person only meeting or event checklist

Use for meetings and events where all participants attend in the same physical location.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Check the route into the room, including doorways, ramps, elevators, and clear paths for mobility devices
    • Check seating, tables, and sightlines so participants can see speakers, screens, and each other
    • Check access to washrooms, emergency exits, and any safety supports participants may need

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot enter, navigate, or leave the space independently.
    • Mobility devices, service animals, or accessibility equipment cannot be accommodated.
    • Seating, tables, or room layouts block access or participation.
    • Participants cannot see, hear, or access key information from their location in the room.
    • Accessibility features or supports are unavailable when needed.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Share entrance, elevator, washroom, and parking or transit details in the invitation, not just the room number.
    • Include a contact participants can reach if they need help finding or accessing the room.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know where to go or how to access the room.
    • Participants arrive without information about entrances, elevators, washrooms, parking, or transit access.
    • Participants do not know who to contact if they experience an access issue.
    • Important access information is only shared verbally or too late.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Point out accessible exits, washrooms, and evacuation routes at the start, not just visually — say it out loud too.
    • Confirm who will assist a participant who cannot evacuate independently, and how.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot find accessible exits, washrooms, or safety supports.
    • Emergency information is only posted visually or only explained verbally.
    • Participants who need assistance do not know what support is available.
    • Safety instructions are unclear, incomplete, or unavailable in an accessible format.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Test audio and visual equipment in the actual room beforehand, not just on paper.
    • Confirm a backup plan (spare microphone, alternate device) in case equipment fails.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot hear speakers clearly.
    • Captions, interpretation, or assistive listening supports are missing or hard to access.
    • Audio, display, or support equipment does not work during the event.
    • There is no backup plan if accessibility supports fail.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use accessible document structure: headings, lists, meaningful link text, and sufficient colour contrast.
    • Share materials in an accessible format (structured Word, HTML, or tagged PDF), and share in advance when possible.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot access slides, documents, agendas, or handouts with assistive technology.
    • Important information is only available in one format.
    • Participants do not have enough time to review complex materials.
    • Visual information is not available in text or another accessible format.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Pass or point a microphone to whoever is speaking, including people asking questions from the audience.
    • This keeps audio clear for captions, interpretation, and assistive listening devices.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot hear speakers or questions clearly.
    • People farther from the speaker miss important information.
    • Captions, interpretation, or assistive listening supports are less accurate because audio is unclear.
    • Remote or hybrid participants miss in-room questions or comments.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask speakers to avoid talking over each other — overlapping speech breaks captions and interpretation.
    • If discussion gets lively, have the moderator briefly step in to restore turn-taking.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot follow the discussion when people speak over each other.
    • Captions and interpretation become inaccurate or incomplete.
    • Participants do not know who is speaking.
    • People who need more time to process information miss key points.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Describe the purpose of what's shown (for example, the main point of a printed handout or demonstration), not every visual detail.
    • If something is only shown in the room, also say it out loud so remote or non-sighted participants don't miss it.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Important information is only shown visually and not explained.
    • Participants who cannot see the room, printed materials, or displayed instructions miss key information.
    • Participants cannot understand charts, diagrams, images, or demonstrations shown in the room.
    • People relying on captions, transcripts, or notes do not receive the full meaning of the content.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • State clearly at the start how to ask a question (for example, raise a hand, use a mic, or contact a moderator).
    • Name the support contact so participants know who to reach if they hit a barrier.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know how to ask questions or request help.
    • Participants are expected to use only one participation method that may not work for them.
    • Accessibility issues are not reported because the support process is unclear.
    • Questions or support requests are missed during the event.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Stop or slow down, fix the issue if possible (repeat information, adjust audio), or switch to your backup plan.
    • Do not continue until you have confirmed with the participant that the issue has been resolved.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing and activating a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants continue to miss information after an access issue is reported.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, visuals, or participation tools fail without a response.
    • Participants do not know whether the issue is being addressed.
    • The meeting continues in a way that excludes some participants.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use headings, lists, and meaningful link text so notes work with assistive technology.
    • Send follow-up promptly — participants who could not fully follow the event need it as soon as possible.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants miss key decisions, links, or next steps if they could not fully follow the event.
    • Participants who could not attend do not have access to the same information.
    • Follow-up materials are shared in formats that are difficult to use with assistive technology.
    • Important information is only available from memory, chat, or spoken discussion.

1.2  Virtual only meeting or event checklist

Use for meetings and events where all participants join remotely.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Test the link yourself before sending it, and include a phone/dial-in backup in case the platform doesn't work for someone.
    • Send joining instructions early enough that participants can troubleshoot before the meeting starts.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot find or use the meeting link.
    • Participants cannot join by phone if the online platform does not work for them.
    • Participants miss the start of the meeting because joining instructions are unclear.
    • Participants do not know what to do if they have technical or accessibility issues joining.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Check this before sending the invitation, not after someone asks — confirm captions, chat, Q&A, and phone participation all work as expected.
    • Tell participants which features are available so they know what to expect.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know whether captions, chat, Q&A, raised hands, or phone participation are available.
    • Participants are expected to use features that may not work with their assistive technology.
    • Organizers discover too late that a needed feature is unavailable or inaccessible.
    • Participants have only one way to participate, and it does not work for everyone.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Share slides, agendas, or documents ahead of time in an accessible format (structured Word, HTML, or tagged PDF).
    • Sharing in advance doesn't replace accessible delivery — still describe key visuals live.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot access slides, agendas, documents, or links during the live session.
    • Participants do not have enough time to review complex information.
    • Participants miss information that is only shared through screen sharing.
    • Participants using assistive technology cannot follow along if materials are not accessible.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • If this is a recurring meeting with the same regular participants, a full walkthrough usually isn't needed each time
    • Give a quick explanation when new participants join, when the platform or process changes, or at the start of a new recurring series.
    • Repeat instructions if participants join partway through or the meeting runs long.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • New or occasional participants do not know how to turn on captions or use participation features.
    • Participants cannot ask questions because the process is unclear.
    • Participants miss information if instructions are only given once and never repeated for newcomers.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say explicitly that video is optional — don't leave participants guessing or feeling pressured.
    • Camera use can affect comfort, privacy, bandwidth, and fatigue, so make it a genuine choice.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants feel pressured to use video when it is not needed.
    • Participants experience fatigue, discomfort, privacy concerns, or bandwidth issues from unnecessary camera use.
    • Participants cannot take part fully because video expectations are unclear.
    • Participation is treated as less valid when someone chooses not to use a camera.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Describe the key message or trend, not every detail — for example, “This chart shows registrations increased steadily.”
    • If names, dates, or decisions appear only on screen, say them out loud too.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Important information is only shown on screen and not explained.
    • Participants who cannot see the screen or shared content miss key information.
    • Participants cannot understand charts, diagrams, demonstrations, images, or screen-shared instructions.
    • People relying on captions, transcripts, or notes do not receive the full meaning of the visual content.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Don't rely on one channel — combine speech, chat, and accessible documents for anything essential.
    • Participants using captions, phone access, or assistive technology may miss information shared only one way.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants miss important information if it is only spoken aloud.
    • Participants miss information if it is only posted in chat.
    • Participants cannot follow when information is only shared through screen sharing.
    • Participants who use captions, assistive technology, or phone participation do not receive the same information.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use headings, lists, and meaningful links so follow-up materials work with assistive technology.
    • Include anything that was only discussed verbally or shown on screen during the live session.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants miss key decisions, links, or next steps if they could not fully follow the live meeting.
    • Participants who could not attend do not have access to the same information.
    • Important information is only available from memory, chat, or spoken discussion.
    • Follow-up materials are shared in formats that are difficult to use with assistive technology.

1.3  Hybrid meeting or event checklist

Use for meetings and events with both in-person and remote participants.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Map out, before the event, exactly how each piece of information (slides, questions, decisions) will reach both audiences equally.
    • Avoid designing an activity that only works for people in the room, or only for people online.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote participants do not receive the same information as people in the room.
    • In-person participants and remote participants have different ways to participate.
    • Essential information is only shared verbally, visually, in the room, or online.
    • Some participants cannot access supports, documents, questions, or discussion in the same way.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Check the physical route into the room, accessible washrooms, and evacuation routes ahead of time.
    • Make sure this information is also available to remote participants who may attend part of the event in person later.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • In-person participants cannot enter, navigate, or leave the space independently.
    • Participants cannot find accessible washrooms, exits, or safety supports.
    • Emergency or safety information is not available in an accessible format.
    • Room access barriers are discovered too late to fix before the event.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Test the full setup together, not each piece separately, confirm remote participants can hear in-room speakers and vice versa if hybrid.
    • Test captions, interpretation, audio, screen sharing, and participation tools together, using the actual event setup.
    • For public, recorded, high-profile, or high-risk events, consider involving accessibility specialists or test users.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Captions, interpretation, audio, video, screen sharing, or participation tools fail during the event.
    • Technical issues are discovered only once participants have joined.
    • Accessibility features that work in a small test don't hold up with a full, large, or hybrid audience.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Make sure accessibility services reach both audiences equally — not just whichever group is easier to support.
    • Confirm how each group accesses the same service (for example, captions on a shared screen vs. captions in the online platform).

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Accessibility services are available to one audience but not the other.
    • Participants do not know how to access captions, CART, ASL/LSQ, interpretation, or materials.
    • Participants using different access methods receive incomplete or different information.
    • Support is not available when participants experience access issues.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Assign separate people to monitor the room and the virtual platform — one person usually can't do both.
    • Make sure someone is specifically responsible for accessibility services (captions, interpretation) during the event.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • No one is monitoring remote participation or in-room participation.
    • Questions, chat messages, raised hands, or support requests are missed.
    • Accessibility or technical issues are reported but no one is assigned to respond.
    • One person is expected to manage too many tasks at once.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Decide in advance who will troubleshoot and how you'll notify participants if something fails.
    • For technical failures, audio (in-room, online, or both), captions, interpretation, participation tools, platform, or livestream, have a fallback ready (phone line, alternate device, or secondary streaming link) so the event doesn't stall while you fix the issue.
    • For booked accessibility services (captioning, interpretation), line up a standby provider you can call on short notice.
    • Decide in advance who is authorized to make the call to pause, switch, or reschedule.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The meeting continues even though some participants cannot hear, see, follow, or participate because no one activates a planned response.
    • Participants do not know what to do when access issues occur, or when a session suddenly goes offline.
    • Organizers cannot quickly switch to another way of sharing information or supporting participation.
    • A vendor cancellation, technical failure, or livestream outage leaves the event without a needed service and no standby ready.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Give both audiences the same instructions for asking questions and requesting help — don't leave remote participants guessing.
    • Repeat instructions partway through longer hybrid sessions, since people join at different times.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know how to ask questions or request support.
    • Remote participants and in-person participants receive different participation instructions.
    • Participants are expected to use only one participation method that may not work for them.
    • Accessibility issues are not reported because the support process is unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say explicitly that video is optional — don't leave participants guessing or feeling pressured.
    • Camera use can affect comfort, privacy, bandwidth, and fatigue, so make it a genuine choice.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants feel pressured to use video when it is not needed.
    • Participants experience fatigue, discomfort, privacy concerns, or bandwidth issues from unnecessary camera use.
    • Participants cannot take part fully because video expectations are unclear.
    • Participation is treated as less valid when someone chooses not to use a camera.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Pass a microphone to anyone asking a question in the room so remote participants and captions pick it up clearly.
    • Without this, remote participants often miss in-room questions and comments entirely.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote participants cannot hear people speaking in the room.
    • Captions or interpretation are inaccurate because room audio is unclear.
    • Participants using assistive listening supports miss in-room questions or comments.
    • People farther from the speaker cannot hear the discussion clearly.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say the question out loud again before answering it, even if it was already audible in the room.
    • This keeps captions, interpretation, and remote participants in sync with the discussion.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote participants miss questions or comments from the room.
    • Participants cannot follow the answer because they did not hear the question.
    • Captions, transcripts, or notes do not capture the full discussion.
    • Remote participants feel excluded from in-room discussion.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say what it is and its key point out loud (for example, “this chart shows a steady increase”), even in a casual setting.
    • Don't assume everyone can see what's being passed around or shared on a small screen.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Something shown informally is not explained to everyone in the discussion.
    • Participants who cannot see what is being shown or passed around miss key information.
    • Participants cannot understand a chart, document, or object shared without warning.
    • People relying on captions, transcripts, or phone participation do not receive the full meaning.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Assign this monitoring to a specific person, the host or presenter usually can't watch everything while running the session.
    • Check in on captions, chat, in-room questions, and language quality on a regular basis, not just at the start.
    • Make it easy for participants to flag an issue as soon as it happens.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote raised hands, chat messages, or Q&A submissions, or accessibility issues are missed.
    • In-room access issues go unnoticed while the online platform is being monitored.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, or language channels fail without anyone noticing.
    • One audience or language group has more opportunity to participate than the other.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Stop and fix the issue, or switch to the backup plan, as soon as any barrier is reported.
    • Announce the pause out loud and through other accessible channels in use (chat, room display), so no audience is left confused.
    • Don't let the event continue if one audience or group is excluded, even if others are unaffected.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing and activating a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants continue to miss information after an access issue is reported.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, visuals, or participation tools fail without a response.
    • A large or hybrid audience doesn't know why the session paused if it isn't clearly announced.
    • The meeting continues in a way that excludes some participants.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask both audiences separately — feedback from only one group can hide barriers the other group experienced.
    • Look for gaps in room setup, remote access, or support roles that affected one audience more than the other, and record what to change for your next hybrid event.

    Related guidance:

    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Feedback only reflects one audience’s experience.
    • Remote access issues or in-room access issues are missed.
    • Organizers do not learn whether participation was equitable for both audiences.
    • Recurring barriers are not identified or addressed.

2.  Meeting and event type checklists

2.1  Audience of 1–25 — checklist

Use for 1–25 participants. Add session-feature and additional-consideration checklists as applicable; small does not mean low risk.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Decide who is responsible for running the meeting and responding to access issues, even informally.
    • Make sure there's a backup if that person is unavailable.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • No one is clearly responsible for running the meeting or responding to access issues.
    • Participants do not know who to contact if they need help.
    • Accessibility support depends on one person without a backup.
    • Questions, support requests, or technical issues are missed because roles are unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Briefly outline the format and how to ask questions or raise concerns, even for an informal meeting.
    • This helps participants know what to expect instead of guessing as the meeting goes.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know what to expect or how to take part.
    • Participants are unsure how to ask questions, raise concerns, or request support.
    • Important participation instructions are only given once or only in one format.
    • Participants miss information because the meeting process is unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use accessible formatting (headings, readable text, sufficient contrast) even for quick or informal documents.
    • Don't skip accessible formatting just because the meeting feels casual — barriers are the same either way.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot access agendas, documents, slides, or data with assistive technology.
    • Materials are shared in a format that is difficult to read, navigate, or understand.
    • Because the meeting feels informal, accessible formatting gets skipped entirely.
    • Participants who need an accessible format have no way to ask for one in time.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • A quick reminder (“one at a time, please”) keeps captions and interpretation accurate during casual back-and-forth.
    • Informal discussions tend to slip into overlapping talk faster than structured ones — watch for it.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Casual back-and-forth discussion makes it hard to follow who is speaking.
    • Captions and interpretation become inaccurate when people talk over each other.
    • Participants who process speech more slowly lose track of the conversation.
    • Without a facilitator reminder, informal meetings tend to slip into overlapping talk.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Repeat or summarize key points, especially decisions or action items, rather than assuming they landed the first time.
    • A quick “does that make sense so far?” check-in costs little and catches missed information early.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who need more time to process information lose track if points are not repeated.
    • Quiet or last-minute check-ins are skipped because the meeting feels informal.
    • Participants are unsure whether they missed something important.
    • Small, casual meetings often skip confirming understanding altogether.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Send a short written summary of decisions, action items, and next steps, even after an informal meeting.
    • For meetings with clients, partners, or other external participants, follow up directly on any questions or issues that were not fully resolved.
    • Share follow-up information in an accessible format so participants can easily refer back to it.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Decisions, action items, or commitments are forgotten after the meeting.
    • Participants who process information best in writing have no record to refer back to.
    • Questions raised during or after the meeting do not receive a clear response.
    • Participants who missed the meeting have no way to catch up on key information.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Circle back personally with clients, partners, or external attendees — a personal note reinforces the relationship in a way a group summary alone doesn't.
    • Don't assume a casual “I'll get back to you” is enough without an actual follow-up.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants assume no one will follow up once an informal meeting ends.
    • Questions raised casually, such as in passing or after the meeting, get forgotten.
    • Participants do not receive a clear answer or resolution.
    • There is no record of what was asked or answered.

2.2  Training, workshops, and presentations - checklist

Use for: training sessions, workshops, briefings, demonstrations, and other sessions where content, slides, or participant learning are central.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • State what participants should know or be able to do by the end of the session.
    • Share the agenda in advance so participants using assistive technology or captions can prepare.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know what the session will cover or what is expected of them.
    • Participants cannot prepare or review materials in advance.
    • Content moves ahead of what participants can process without warning.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use accessible document structure: headings, lists, meaningful link text, and sufficient colour contrast.
    • Share materials in advance when possible so participants can review or use their own assistive technology.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot access slides, handouts, or activity materials with assistive technology.
    • Participants do not have enough time to review dense or complex training content.
    • Materials shared only during the session leave no time to prepare questions.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Walk presenters through describing what's on screen out loud, not just pointing or clicking silently.
    • Ask presenters to slow down during live demonstrations so captions and interpretation can keep up.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot follow live demonstrations or on-screen steps that are not described.
    • Captions or interpretation fall behind during fast-paced demonstrations.
    • Participants using assistive technology miss key steps shown only visually.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Schedule short breaks for longer sessions, and build extra time into the agenda for questions and processing.
    • Avoid packing the agenda so tightly that questions or breaks get cut.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants experience fatigue or cognitive overload from dense content without breaks.
    • There is not enough time to ask questions or process new information.
    • Participants using captions, interpretation, or assistive technology fall behind a rushed agenda.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Allow participants to respond by voice, chat, or another accessible method rather than only through one tool.
    • Give enough time for participants to read, think, and respond before moving on.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants have only one way to take part, and it does not work for everyone.
    • There is not enough time to think or respond to an activity.
    • Participants are excluded from polls or quizzes that rely on a single inaccessible tool.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask a quick "does this make sense so far?" before moving to the next section.
    • Repeat or summarize key points rather than assuming everyone caught them the first time.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who need more time to process information lose track of dense training content.
    • Participants are unsure whether they missed something important.
    • Training moves ahead before questions or confusion are addressed.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use headings, lists, and meaningful link text so follow-up materials work with assistive technology.
    • Include anything demonstrated live that was not already in the shared materials.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who could not fully follow the live session miss key content.
    • Follow-up materials are shared in a format that is difficult to use with assistive technology.
    • Participants who could not attend do not have access to the same information.

2.3  Larger meeting (26 to 100 participants) - checklist

Use for 26–100 participants. Add the high-risk or testing checklist and any selected session features and considerations.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • For in-person attendance, provide the location, accessible arrival route, room details, and who to contact for assistance.
    • For remote attendance, provide the meeting link, available dial-in option, access codes, and plain-language joining steps.
    • Explain the alternative if the main arrival or joining method is unavailable.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot find the location or join remotely because access instructions are missing or unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Check the platform's participant limits before the event, especially if your expected number is close to a known threshold.
    • Features that work fine in a small test can behave differently with a full, large audience.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The platform slows down, drops connections, or loses features under a large number of participants.
    • Technical issues are discovered only once the full audience has joined.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Split responsibilities between participant questions, accessibility requests, and technical issues as needed.
    • For online participation, name who monitors chat or Q&A; for in-person attendance, name who monitors the room and handles microphones.
    • Give the support team a clear way to alert the host without talking over the session.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The host cannot present and monitor every access or participation issue at the same time.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Allow space for mobility aids and support people, and keep accessible routes clear.
    • Check that participants can see displays and any interpreters, and hear the speakers.

    Related guidance:

    • Accessible meetings and events guidance (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • A larger audience blocks accessible routes or cannot see or hear essential information.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask speakers to briefly state their name when they begin speaking or take over the discussion (for example, “This is Martyna speaking.”).
    • This matters most when there are several speakers or when someone joins partway through.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot tell who is speaking when there are several presenters.
    • Captions, interpretation, or transcripts do not identify who is speaking.
    • Participants who join partway through a session cannot follow who is presenting.
    • Handoffs between speakers feel abrupt or unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say the question out loud before answering, even if you think everyone heard or saw it.
    • This keeps captions, interpretation, and the answer connected to its original question.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who cannot hear the person asking miss the context for the answer.
    • Captions and interpretation cannot capture a question that is never spoken aloud.
    • Participants relying on audio only do not know a question was typed in chat.
    • An answer without its question is difficult to follow for many participants.

2.4  Town hall, organization-wide session, or audience of 101 or more — checklist

Use for 101 or more participants, or a town hall or organization-wide session at any size. Add selected session features and considerations.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • For in-person attendance, provide the location, accessible arrival route, room details, and who to contact for assistance.
    • For remote attendance, provide the meeting link, available dial-in option, access codes, and plain-language joining steps.
    • Explain the alternative if the main arrival or joining method is unavailable.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot find the location or join remotely because access instructions are missing or unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Check the platform's participant limits before the event, especially if your expected number is close to a known threshold.
    • Features that work fine in a small test can behave differently with a full, large audience.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The platform slows down, drops connections, or loses features under a large number of participants.
    • Technical issues are discovered only once the full audience has joined.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Split responsibilities between participant questions, accessibility requests, and technical issues as needed.
    • For online participation, name who monitors chat or Q&A; for in-person attendance, name who monitors the room and handles microphones.
    • Give the support team a clear way to alert the host without talking over the session.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The host cannot present and monitor every access or participation issue at the same time.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Decide in advance who will troubleshoot and how you'll notify participants if something fails.
    • For technical failures, audio (in-room, online, or both), captions, interpretation, participation tools, platform, or livestream, have a fallback ready (phone line, alternate device, or secondary streaming link) so the event doesn't stall while you fix the issue.
    • For booked accessibility services (captioning, interpretation), line up a standby provider you can call on short notice.
    • Decide in advance who is authorized to make the call to pause, switch, or reschedule.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The meeting continues even though some participants cannot hear, see, follow, or participate because no one activates a planned response.
    • Participants do not know what to do when access issues occur, or when a session suddenly goes offline.
    • Organizers cannot quickly switch to another way of sharing information or supporting participation.
    • A vendor cancellation, technical failure, or livestream outage leaves the event without a needed service and no standby ready.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Allow space for mobility aids and support people, and keep accessible routes clear.
    • Check that participants can see displays and any interpreters, and hear the speakers.

    Related guidance:

    • Accessible meetings and events guidance (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • A larger audience blocks accessible routes or cannot see or hear essential information.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • A short verbal introduction (“This is [name], continuing on...”) helps participants, captions, and transcripts track who's speaking.
    • This matters most when there are several speakers or when someone joins partway through.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot tell who is speaking when there are several presenters.
    • Captions, interpretation, or transcripts do not identify who is speaking.
    • Participants who join partway through a session cannot follow who is presenting.
    • Handoffs between speakers feel abrupt or unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Name the main question route, such as a roving microphone in the room or a moderated online Q&A channel.
    • Tell participants how to submit a question if they cannot use the main route.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Questions are lost or inaccessible when participants do not know which route to use.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Have a moderator collect questions and manage speaking turns.
    • Use the room microphone and any online question channels as appropriate, and allow time for captions or interpretation if used.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Overlapping or rapid questions prevent participants from following or contributing.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Assign this monitoring to a specific person, the host or presenter usually can't watch everything while running the session.
    • Check in on captions, chat, in-room questions, and language quality on a regular basis, not just at the start.
    • Make it easy for participants to flag an issue as soon as it happens.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote raised hands, chat messages, or Q&A submissions, or accessibility issues are missed.
    • In-room access issues go unnoticed while the online platform is being monitored.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, or language channels fail without anyone noticing.
    • One audience or language group has more opportunity to participate than the other.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Stop and fix the issue, or switch to the backup plan, as soon as any barrier is reported.
    • Announce the pause out loud and through other accessible channels in use (chat, room display), so no audience is left confused.
    • Don't let the event continue if one audience or group is excluded, even if others are unaffected.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing and activating a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants continue to miss information after an access issue is reported.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, visuals, or participation tools fail without a response.
    • A large or hybrid audience doesn't know why the session paused if it isn't clearly announced.
    • The meeting continues in a way that excludes some participants.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say the question out loud before answering, even if you think everyone heard or saw it.
    • This keeps captions, interpretation, and the answer connected to its original question.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who cannot hear the person asking miss the context for the answer.
    • Captions and interpretation cannot capture a question that is never spoken aloud.
    • Participants relying on audio only do not know a question was typed in chat.
    • An answer without its question is difficult to follow for many participants.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Send follow-up soon after the event — large groups can't casually ask each other what they missed the way small groups can.
    • Make sure the same materials reach everyone, not just those who ask.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants in a large group cannot informally ask each other what they missed.
    • Follow-up sent late leaves many participants without timely information.
    • Materials shared only with some attendees exclude others in a large audience.
    • Participants across different roles or locations have no other way to catch up.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Watch for the same issue reported by more than one person — that's a signal worth prioritizing.
    • A single comment is easy to miss; a repeated pattern across a large audience is not.

    Related guidance:

    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • A single piece of feedback is easy to overlook, but a repeated pattern is not.
    • Large events generate more feedback, making it easy to miss recurring issues.
    • Without looking for patterns, the same accessibility issue can repeat at every future event.
    • Prioritizing widely reported issues has the biggest impact on future participants.

2.5  Public, formal, or high-risk events checklist

Use for: public events, high-profile events, formal sessions, technical briefings, legal or policy-heavy events, bilingual events, interpreted events, and recorded events.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Make sure registration forms, email invitations, websites, and event documents work with assistive technology and can be completed without a mouse.
    • Clearly explain available accessibility supports, such as captions, interpretation, alternate formats, or accommodation request processes.
    • Use plain language and avoid unexplained acronyms, technical terms, or complex instructions when communicating with participants.
    • Provide important event information early enough for participants to request accommodations, review materials, and prepare to participate.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Accommodations and follow-up (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot complete registration forms or access event information using assistive technology.
    • Participants do not know what accessibility supports are available or how to request them.
    • Important information is inaccessible, unclear, or provided too late for participants to prepare.
    • Participants miss critical event details because communications use complex language or inaccessible formats.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Offer at least one alternative to an online form (email, phone, or a named contact).
    • This ensures people who cannot use a particular tool or format are not excluded from registering.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants are blocked if one registration method is inaccessible or does not work for them.
    • Participants cannot ask questions because only one contact or tool is available.
    • People who cannot use a web form, chat, or online tool have no alternative.
    • Access needs or questions are missed because the response process is too limited.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask about accommodation needs during registration, with enough lead time to book services like CART or ASL/LSQ.
    • Some accessibility services need several weeks' notice — build that into your timeline.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Accessibility services are requested too late to arrange.
    • Participants do not know how to request accommodations or alternate formats.
    • Organizers do not have enough time to book captions, CART, ASL/LSQ, interpretation, or other supports.
    • Participants arrive without the supports they need to take part.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Turn accommodation requests into a firm decision on services (CART, ASL/LSQ, interpretation) well before the event.
    • For public or official events, consider higher-accuracy services even if no one has requested them yet.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Services are chosen without considering the public or official visibility of the event.
    • Registrant accommodation requests are collected but never translated into a final decision.
    • Higher-accuracy services, such as CART, are not considered for high-profile or official events.
    • Participants find out too late which accessibility services will or will not be available.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Send agendas, slides, names, and acronyms to captioners and interpreters ahead of time.
    • Better preparation means fewer errors in captions, interpretation, and the final transcript.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)
    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Captioners or interpreters do not have key terms, names, acronyms, or technical language in advance.
    • Captions, interpretation, or transcripts are less accurate.
    • Service providers cannot prepare for specialized, bilingual, or high-risk content.
    • Participants receive incomplete or unclear access to the event content.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Name one person as the point of contact for outside vendors during the event.
    • Confirm that person has the authority to make quick decisions if a vendor issue comes up live.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • No one is responsible for communicating with outside vendors during the event.
    • A vendor issue goes unresolved because no one has the authority to make a quick decision.
    • Delays happen while staff figure out who should contact the service provider.
    • External providers have no single point of contact for last-minute changes.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Test the full setup together, not each piece separately, confirm remote participants can hear in-room speakers and vice versa if hybrid.
    • Test captions, interpretation, audio, screen sharing, and participation tools together, using the actual event setup.
    • For public, recorded, high-profile, or high-risk events, consider involving accessibility specialists or test users.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Captions, interpretation, audio, video, screen sharing, or participation tools fail during the event.
    • Technical issues are discovered only once participants have joined.
    • Accessibility features that work in a small test don't hold up with a full, large, or hybrid audience.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Rehearse with speakers, moderators, interpreters, and captioners together so everyone knows their role.
    • This is where you catch pacing or technical issues before they happen live.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Speakers do not know how to describe visuals, pace delivery, or support captions and interpretation.
    • Moderators, interpreters, captioners, and support staff are unsure of their roles.
    • Technical or accessibility issues are discovered during the live event instead of before it.
    • The event moves too quickly for participants using captions, interpretation, or assistive technologies.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Decide in advance who will troubleshoot and how you'll notify participants if something fails.
    • For technical failures, audio (in-room, online, or both), captions, interpretation, participation tools, platform, or livestream, have a fallback ready (phone line, alternate device, or secondary streaming link) so the event doesn't stall while you fix the issue.
    • For booked accessibility services (captioning, interpretation), line up a standby provider you can call on short notice.
    • Decide in advance who is authorized to make the call to pause, switch, or reschedule.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The meeting continues even though some participants cannot hear, see, follow, or participate because no one activates a planned response.
    • Participants do not know what to do when access issues occur, or when a session suddenly goes offline.
    • Organizers cannot quickly switch to another way of sharing information or supporting participation.
    • A vendor cancellation, technical failure, or livestream outage leaves the event without a needed service and no standby ready.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • State clearly, on the record, that captioning, interpretation, or other accessibility services are available.
    • Public and formal events often need this announced explicitly, not assumed.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Press, officials, or public observers are not told that accessibility services are available.
    • Participants who join a formal or public event expect an official opening announcement.
    • Services go unused simply because attendees did not know they existed.
    • Public-facing events need this information stated clearly and on the record.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Pin or spotlight the interpreter's video so they aren't hidden by shared slides or other content.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants who use sign language interpretation cannot see the interpreter.
    • Interpreter video is hidden, too small, or replaced by shared content.
    • Participants miss information when speakers, slides, or videos change the screen layout.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Stop and fix the issue, or switch to the backup plan, as soon as any barrier is reported.
    • Announce the pause out loud and through other accessible channels in use (chat, room display), so no audience is left confused.
    • Don't let the event continue if one audience or group is excluded, even if others are unaffected.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing and activating a backup plan (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants continue to miss information after an access issue is reported.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, visuals, or participation tools fail without a response.
    • A large or hybrid audience doesn't know why the session paused if it isn't clearly announced.
    • The meeting continues in a way that excludes some participants.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Keep a written record of accessibility feedback and what was changed as a result.
    • This documentation supports accountability for recurring or high-profile events.

    Related guidance:

    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Feedback from a high-profile event is not documented for accountability or audit purposes.
    • Recurring formal events repeat the same accessibility issues without a documented history.
    • Improvements made are not tracked, so progress cannot be demonstrated over time.
    • Without documentation, there is no official basis for future planning decisions.

3.  Add-on checklists

The core accessibility and accommodations checklists apply to every planning path. Other checklists are added from audience size, session features, and the additional considerations in question 3. The wizard filters individual actions to match delivery and selected needs.

3.1  Core accessibility checklist

Included in every planning path.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Use simple, familiar words where possible. Keep sentences short, explain acronyms on first use, and avoid jargon, idioms, and unnecessary technical language.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Confusion caused by jargon.
    • Cognitive overload.
    • Difficulty understanding complex information.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Note what worked, what didn't, and what you'll change next time — even a quick written note helps.
    • Look for issues that keep coming up across meetings or events so you can fix the root cause.

    Related guidance:

    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The same accessibility issues happen again in future meetings or events.
    • Reported barriers are not documented or addressed.
    • Future planning does not benefit from what was learned.

3.2  Accessibility contact and follow-up checklist

Included in every planning path.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • For a small or informal meeting, the host may be the accessibility contact.
    • For a public, formal, or larger event, identify a specific contact and include their contact information in the invitation, registration page, or agenda.
    • Provide enough notice when accommodations or accessibility services need time to arrange.

    Related guidance:

    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know who to contact if they need accessibility help or an accommodation.
    • Accessibility requests are missed or received too late to arrange.
    • Participants must raise accessibility needs publicly during the meeting.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • For a small or medium group, answer individually in writing as soon as possible after the event.
    • For a large audience or town hall, compile unanswered questions into one written response and share it with everyone — individual follow-up usually isn't realistic at that scale.
    • Share the answer with the wider group if it's likely relevant to others too.

    Related guidance:

    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)
    • Sharing recordings, transcripts, and follow-up materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not receive answers if there was not enough time during the event.
    • Questions asked through chat, Q&A, or another method are missed.
    • Participants who need more time to process information lose the chance to follow up.
    • For large audiences, individually following up with every participant is not realistic, and unanswered questions are simply forgotten instead of being compiled and shared.

3.3  Bilingual and official languages checklist

Use when the meeting or event is bilingual, interpreted, or involves both official languages.

Before
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Decide this early — it affects materials, staffing, and how much lead time you need.
    • Share this decision with participants as soon as it's confirmed.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know which language or languages will be used.
    • Participants do not know whether interpretation or bilingual participation will be available.
    • Participants cannot prepare because the language format is unclear.
    • Language needs are discovered too late to arrange support.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Tell participants which interpretation option is available (for example, simultaneous interpretation or bilingual summaries) and how to access it.
    • Confirm interpreters will be visible and audible before the event starts.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know how to access interpretation.
    • Participants join the wrong language channel or miss interpretation instructions.
    • Interpreters are not visible, audible, or available when needed.
    • Participants miss information because interpretation setup is unclear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • State the language format (English, French, bilingual, interpreted) directly in the invitation — don't leave participants to guess.
    • Clearly state the language format (English, French, bilingual, or interpreted) in the invitation, agenda, and joining instructions so participants can plan their participation and request support if needed.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants receive language information too late.
    • Participants do not know whether materials, discussion, or questions will be bilingual.
    • Participants cannot decide whether they need interpretation or other support.
    • Language instructions are only shared verbally or only during the event.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Prepare both language versions together so neither is late, incomplete, or lower quality.
    • This applies to follow-up materials too, not just the invitation and agenda.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing accessible content and materials (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot access information in the official language of their choice when required or needed.
    • One language version is incomplete, late, or lower quality.
    • Participants cannot prepare because materials are not available in the language they need.
    • Follow-up information is not equally available in both official languages.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Give clear, simple steps for finding and using the correct language channel or interpretation tool.
    • Test the tool yourself first so your instructions match what participants will actually see.

    Related guidance:

    • Choosing an accessible platform, venue, or tools (opens in a new tab); Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants cannot find or use the correct language channel.
    • Participants miss information while trying to switch language settings.
    • Interpretation tools are not accessible or are difficult to use.
    • Participants do not have a backup option if the language tool does not work.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Ask speakers to say a short phrase before switching (for example, “I will now continue in French”).
    • This gives interpreters, captioners, and participants a moment to adjust.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Language changes happen without warning.
    • Participants, captioners, or interpreters do not have time to adjust.
    • Captions, interpretation, or transcripts become inaccurate when language changes suddenly.
    • Participants miss information because the language change is not clear.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Send a short glossary of names, acronyms, and technical terms to captioners and interpreters in advance.
    • This noticeably reduces errors in captions, interpretation, and the final transcript.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Names, acronyms, technical terms, or proper nouns are captioned or interpreted incorrectly.
    • Captioners and interpreters cannot prepare for specialized content.
    • Participants misunderstand key information because terms are inconsistent.
    • Recordings, transcripts, or summaries contain avoidable errors.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Add buffer time in the agenda — bilingual events take longer than unilingual ones.
    • Rushing interpretation or summaries defeats the purpose of providing them.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • The event moves too quickly for participants using interpretation or captions.
    • There is not enough time for bilingual summaries, language transitions, or questions.
    • Participants miss information because interpretation or summaries are rushed.
    • Speakers switch languages or topics before participants have time to follow.
During
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Open the event with a welcome in both official languages, even briefly.
    • This signals from the start that both languages are genuinely supported.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know that both official languages are supported.
    • Participants are unsure whether they may use the official language of their choice.
    • The language approach is unclear at the start of the event.
    • Participants miss early instructions about language or interpretation.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Tell participants they may use the official language of their choice, if that applies.
    • Explain how to access interpretation and how questions in either language will be handled.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Planning and testing accessibility services (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants do not know how to use interpretation or language channels.
    • Participants do not know whether they can ask questions in either official language.
    • Participants miss information because bilingual participation expectations are unclear.
    • Participants cannot access the event fully in the language they need.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Say a brief phrase before switching languages so no one is caught off guard mid-sentence.
    • This keeps captions and interpretation accurate through the transition.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants are surprised by a language change and miss information.
    • Captioners, interpreters, or participants do not have time to adjust.
    • Captions, interpretation, or transcripts become inaccurate.
    • Participants cannot tell which language will be used next.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Slow down slightly and enunciate clearly — this improves caption and interpretation accuracy immediately.
    • A moderate pace also helps participants who process information more slowly.

    Related guidance:

    • Preparing speakers and presenters (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Captions or interpretation become incomplete or inaccurate because speech is too fast.
    • Participants do not have enough time to process information.
    • Participants miss acronyms, names, technical terms, or language changes.
    • People using captions, interpretation, or assistive technologies cannot keep up.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Build extra time into the schedule so interpretation and bilingual summaries aren't rushed.
    • Don't move on before questions in either language have had a chance to be asked.

    Related guidance:

    • Bilingual and official languages delivery (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Participants using interpretation do not have enough time to follow and respond.
    • Bilingual summaries are rushed or skipped.
    • Questions are cut short because language transitions take more time.
    • Participants miss information because the agenda does not account for interpretation or summaries.
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Assign this monitoring to a specific person, the host or presenter usually can't watch everything while running the session.
    • Check in on captions, chat, in-room questions, and language quality on a regular basis, not just at the start.
    • Make it easy for participants to flag an issue as soon as it happens.

    Related guidance:

    • Assigning roles and support (opens in a new tab)
    • Facilitating accessible participation during the event (opens in a new tab)

    Helps prevent barriers such as:

    • Remote raised hands, chat messages, or Q&A submissions, or accessibility issues are missed.
    • In-room access issues go unnoticed while the online platform is being monitored.
    • Captions, interpretation, audio, or language channels fail without anyone noticing.
    • One audience or language group has more opportunity to participate than the other.
After
  • Show guidance and barriers

    How to do this:

    • Send follow-up in both official languages at the same time, in accessible formats.
